readings.c1s1:
¶
'''2.''' Toward the ecclesiastical west. See ''west.''
{{smaller block|Mass is celebrated by the priest standing behind the altar with his face ''westward.''
{{right|''E. A. Freeman'', Venice, p. 105.}}}}

{{smaller|'''Westward ho!''' to the west: an old cry of London watermen on the Thames in hailing passengers bound westward, taken as the title of a play by Dekker and Webster and of a novel by Charles Kingsley.}}
{{smaller block|<poem>''Oli.'' There lies your way, due west.
''Vio.'' Then ''westward-ho!''</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', T. N., iii. 1. 146.}}}}

'''westward''' (west′wärd), ''a.'' [< ''westward, adv.''] Being toward the west; bearing or tending westward: as, a ''westward'' position or course; the ''westward'' trend of the mountains.

'''westwardly''' (west′wärd-li), ''a.'' [< ''westward'' + ''-ly''<sup>1</sup>.] Bearing toward or from the west; westerly. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|On the 19th, the [ice-]pack was driven in by a ''westwardly'' wind, and . . . this open space was closed.
{{right|''C. F. Hall'', Polar Expedition, p. 259.}}}}

'''westwardly''' (west′wärd-li), ''adv.'' [< ''westwardly, a.''] In a direction bearing toward the west: as, to pass ''westwardly.''

'''westwards''' (west′wärdz), ''adv.'' [< ME. *''westwardes'' (= D. ''westwaarts'' = G. ''westwärts''); as ''westward'' + adv. gen. ''-s''.] Same as ''westward.''

'''westy<sup>1</sup>†''', ''a.'' [ME., also ''westiȝ'', < AS. ''wēstig'', desert, < ''wēste'', a desert, waste: see ''waste''<sup>1</sup>.] Waste; desert. ''Layamon'', l. 1120.

'''westy<sup>2</sup>''' (wes′ti), ''a.'' Dizzy; giddy. ''Ray; Halliwell.'' [Prov. Eng.]
{{smaller block|<poem>Whiles he lies wallowing with a ''westy'' head,
And palish carcass, on his brothel bed.</poem>}}
readings.c3s1:
{{smaller|act of celebrating by a convivial supper, on the first Monday in March, the cessation of work by candle-light. ''Halliwell.''}}

'''wet<sup>2</sup>†''', ''v.'' and ''n.'' A Middle English form of ''wit''<sup>1</sup>.

'''wetand†.''' A Middle English present participle of ''wit''<sup>1</sup>.

'''wetandly†''', ''adv.'' A Middle English form of ''wittingly.''

'''wet-bird''' (wet′bėrd), ''n.'' The chaffinch, ''Fringilla cœlebs,'' whose cry is thought to foretell rain. See cut under ''chaffinch.'' [Local, Eng.]

'''wet-broke''' (wet′brōk), ''n.'' In ''paper-manuf.'', the moist and imperfectly felted stock or pulp as it leaves the wire cylinder, and before it has been smoothed out on the forwarding-blanket. ''E. H. Knight.''

'''wet-cup''' (wet′kup), ''n.'' A cupping-glass when used in the operation of wet-cupping. {{smaller|Sometimes it is specially constructed with a lance or scarificator, which can be used to incise the skin after the cup has been applied.}}

'''wet-cupping''' (wet′kup″ing), ''n.'' The application of a cupping-glass simultaneously with incision of the skin, by means of which a small quantity of blood is withdrawn. See ''cupping'', 1.

'''wete†.''' A Middle English form of ''wet''<sup>1</sup>, ''wit''<sup>1</sup>.

'''wether''' (weᴛ̵ʜ′ėr), ''n.'' [E. dial. also ''wedder;'' < ME. ''wether'', ''wethir'', ''wedyr'', < AS. ''wither'', a wether, a castrated ram, = OS. ''withar'', ''wither'' = D. ''wedder'', ''weder'' = OHG. ''widar'', MHG. ''wider'', G. ''widder'' = Icel. ''vethr'' = Sw. ''vädur'' = Dan.
readings.c3s2:
''væder'', ''vædder'', a ram, = Goth. ''withrus'', a lamb; akin to L. ''vitulus'', a calf, Skt. ''vatsa'', calf, young, lit. ‘a yearling,’ connected with Skt. ''vatsara'' and Gr. ἔτος, a year, L. ''vetus'', aged, old: see ''veal'' and ''veteran''.] A castrated ram.
{{smaller block|And softer than the wolle is of a ''wether''.
{{right|''Chaucer'', Miller’s Tale, l. 63.}}}}

'''wether-hog''' (weᴛ̵ʜ′ėr-hog), ''n.'' A young wether. [Prov. Eng.]

'''wethewynde†''', ''n.'' A Middle English form of ''withwind''.

'''wetly''' (wet′li), ''adv.'' [< ''wet''<sup>1</sup> + ''-ly''<sup>2</sup>.] In a wet state or condition; moistly.
{{smaller block|“Love,” she says, very sweetly, while, for the last time, her blue eyes ''wetly'' dwell on his.
{{right|''Rhoda Broughton'', Joan, ii. 11.}}}}

'''wetness''' (wet′nes), ''n.'' The state or condition of being wet; also, the capacity for communicating moisture or making wet: as, the ''wetness'' of the atmosphere or of steam.
{{smaller block|The ''wetness'' of the working fluid [steam] to which the action of the walls of the cylinder gives rise is essentially superficial.
{{right|''Encyc. Brit.'', XXII. 488.}}}}

'''wet-nurse''' (wet′nėrs), ''n.'' A woman employed to suckle the infant of another. Compare ''dry-nurse''.

'''wet-nurse''' (wet′nėrs), ''v. t.'' [< ''wet-nurse'', ''n.''] '''1.''' To act as a wet-nurse to; suckle.
{{smaller block|<poem>Or is he a mythus — ancient word for “humbug” —
Such as Livy told about the wolf that ''wet-nursed''
Romulus and Remus?</poem>
{{right|''O. W. Holmes'', Professor, i.}}}}
Hence — '''2.''' To coddle as a wet-nurse does; treat with the tenderness shown to an infant.
readings.c3s4: the blowing-iron by applying a moistened tool to the neck.

'''westy1†''', ''a.''   [ME., also ''westiȝ'', < AS. ''wēstig'', desert, < ''wēste'', a desert, waste: see ''waste''1.]   Waste; desert.   ''Layamon'', l. 1120. '''westy2''' (wes′ti), ''a.'' Dizzy; giddy.   ''Ray; Halliwell.'' [Prov. Eng.] {{smaller block|Whiles he lies wallowing with a ''westy'' head, And palish carcass, on his brothel bed. {{right|''Bp. Hall'', Satires, IV. i. 158.}}}} '''wet1''' (wet), ''a.''   [E. dial. and Sc. also ''weet'' and ''wat''; < ME. ''wet'', ''weet'', ''wat'', < AS. ''wǣt'' = OFries. ''wēt'', ''weit'' = Icel. ''vātr'' = Sw. ''våt'' = Dan. ''vaad'', wet, moist; akin to AS. ''wæter'', etc., water, and to Goth. ''wato'', etc., water: see ''water''.]   '''1.''' Covered with or permeated by a moist or fluid substance; charged with moisture: as, a ''wet'' sponge; ''wet'' land; ''wet'' cheeks; a ''wet'' painting (one on which the paint is still semi-fluid). {{smaller block|Ziff the Erthe were made moyst and ''weet'' with that Watre, it wolde nevere bere Fruyt. {{right|''Mandeville'', Travels, p. 100.}}}} {{smaller block|I, forced to go to the office on foot, was almost ''wet'' to the skin, and spoiled my silk breeches almost. {{right|''Pepys'', Diary, II. 293.}}}} {{smaller block|In the greenest growth of the Maytime, I rode where the woods were ''wet''. {{right|''Swinburne'', An Interlude.}}}} '''2.''' Filled with or containing a supply of water: as, a ''wet'' dock; a ''wet'' meter. See phrases below.—'''3.''' Consisting of water or other liquid; of a watery nature. {{smaller block|Be your tears ''wet''? Yes, ’faith. I pray, weep not. {{right|''Shak.'', Lear, iv. 7. 71.}}}} '''4.''' Characterized by rain; rainy; drizzly; showery: as, ''wet'' weather; a ''wet'' season (used especially with reference to tropical or semitropical countries, in which the year is divided into ''wet'' and ''dry'' seasons). {{smaller block|''Wet'' October’s torrent flood. {{right|''Milton'', Comus, l. 930.}}}} {{smaller block|As to the Seasons of the Year, I cannot distinguish them there [in the torrid zone] no other way than by ''Wet'' and Dry. {{right|''Dampier'', Voyages, II. iii. 2.}}}} '''5.''' Drenched or drunk with liquor; tipsy. [Colloq.] {{smaller block|When my lost Lover the tall Ship ascends,
With Music gay, and ''wet'' with jovial Friends. {{right|''Prior'', Celia to Damon.}}}} '''6.''' In ''U. S. polit. slang'', opposed to prohibition of the manufacture and sale of intoxicating liquors: as, a ''wet'' town. Compare ''dry'', 13.—'''A wet blanket.''' {{smaller|See ''blanket''.}}—'''A wet boat,''' {{smaller|a boat that is crank and ships water readily.}} {{smaller block|“Why don’t you go forward, sir? . . . she is sure to wet us abaft.” . . . “Thank you, but . . . (with an heroic attempt at sea-slang) I like ''a wet boat''.” {{right|''C. Reade'', Love me Little, xvii.}}}} '''A wet day.''' {{smaller|Same as ''a rainy day'' (which see, under ''rainy'').}} {{smaller block|Ergo, saith the miser, “part with nothing, but keep all against ''a wet day''.” {{right|''Fuller'', General Worthies, xi. (''Davies.'')}}}} '''Wet bargain.''' {{smaller|Same as ''Dutch bargain'' (which see, under ''bargain'').}}—'''Wet bob,''' {{smaller|a boy who goes in for boating in preference to cricket, foot-ball, or other land-sports. [Eton College slang.]}} {{smaller block|Everything is enjoyable at Eton in the summer half. The ''wet-bobs'' on the river, in all their many trials of strength, . . . and the “dry-bobs” in the playing-fields, with all the excitement of their countless matches. {{right|''C. E. Pascoe'', Every-day Life in Our Public Schools, p. 62.}}}} '''Wet brain,''' {{smaller|a dropsical condition of the brain and its membranes, sometimes observed in post-mortem examinations of those who have died of delirium tremens.}}—'''Wet-bulb thermometer.''' {{smaller|See ''psychrometer'' (with cut).}}—'''Wet cooper.''' {{smaller|See ''cooper''.}}—'''Wet dock,''' {{smaller|a dock or basin at a seaport furnished with gates for shutting in the tidal water, so as to float vessels berthed in it at a proper level for loading and unloading.}}—'''Wet goods,''' {{smaller|liquors: so called in humorous allusion to ''dry goods.'' [Slang, U. S.]—'''Wet meter''', a gas-meter in which the gas to be measured passes through a body of water. The wet meter regulates the flow of gas more steadily than the dry meter, but is more difficult to keep in order.—'''Wet plate''', in ''photog.'', a plate coated with collodion and sensitized with a salt (usually the nitrate) of silver: so called because it is necessary, in this process, to perform all the operations of making the picture, to and including the final fixing of the plate, before the coating of collodion dries. For some thirty years, from about 1850, this was by far the most important photographic process in use, but it is now almost wholly superseded by the various rapid dry-plate processes. The phrase is also used attributively to note the process or anything connected with it. See ''collodion process'', under ''collodion.''—'''Wet port''', a seaport as a place of entry for foreign goods, in distinction from a ''dry port'', or land-port, a place of entry for goods transported by land.   ''Encyc. Brit.'', VI. 729.—'''Wet preparation''', a specimen of natural history immersed in alcohol or other preservative fluid.—'''Wet provisions''', a class of provisions furnished to a ship, including salt beef and pork, vinegar, molasses, pickles, etc.—'''Wet puddling.''' See ''puddling'', 2.—'''Wet Quaker†''', a Quaker who does not strictly observe the rules of his society.}} {{smaller block|Socinians and Presbyterians, Quakers, and ''Wet-Quakers'', or Merry-ones. {{right|''T. Ward'', England’s Reformation, I. 213.}}}} {{smaller|'''Wet Quakerism.''' See ''Quakerism.''—'''Wet steam.''' See ''steam'' and ''open'', 13.—'''Wet way''', in ''chem.'', the method of qualitative and quantitative analysis and assay in which the substance to be examined is first dissolved in some liquid and then treated with liquid reagents: the opposite of fire-assay, or treatment in the dry way. In the ordinary analysis of minerals, the substance is first finely pulverized and then dissolved in an acid, after which further treatment follows. If insoluble in an acid, it is fused with potassium or sodium carbonate, after which treatment the fused mass is soluble, either wholly or in part, the silica (if the mineral is a silicate) separating out and being removed by filtering, after which the process is continued the same way as when the substance is soluble without the necessity of a preliminary attack by an alkali at a high temperature. Ordinary analyses of minerals are made in the wet way, assays of ores not infrequently in the dry way.—'''With a wet finger'''†, with little effort or trouble; very easily or readily: probably from the practice of wetting the finger to facilitate matters, as in turning over a leaf of a book, or rubbing out writing on a slate.}} {{smaller block|Walk you here; I’ll beckon; you shall see I’ll fetch her ''with a wet finger.'' {{right|''Dekker and Webster'', Westward Ho, ii. 2.}}}} '''wet'''1 (wet), ''n.''   [E. dial. and Sc. also ''weet'' and ''wat''; < ME. ''wet, wete, wæte, wate'', < AS. ''wǣta'', m., ''wǣte'', f. (= Icel. Sw. ''vǣta'' = Dan. ''væde''), wet, moisture, < ''wǣt'', wet: see ''wet''1, ''a.'']   '''1.''' That which makes wet, as water and other liquids; moisture; specifically, rain. {{smaller block|I se wel how ye swete; Have heer a cloth and wype awey the ''wete.'' {{right|''Chaucer'', Canon’s Yeoman’s Tale, l. 176.}}}} {{smaller block|Upon whose [a river’s] weeping margent she was set; Like usury, applying ''wet'' to ''wet.'' {{right|''Shak.'', Lover’s Complaint, l. 40.}}}} {{smaller block|Aft ha’e I run your errands, lady, When blawin baith wind and ''weet.'' {{right|''Lady Maisry'' (Child’s Ballads, II. 83).}}}} {{smaller block|The gable-end of the cottage was stained with ''wet.'' {{right|''T. Hardy'', Three Strangers.}}}} '''2.''' The act of wetting; specifically, a wetting of the throat with drink; a drink or dram of liquor; indulgence in drinking. [Slang.] {{smaller block|No bargain could be completed without a ''wet'', and no friendship or enmity forgotten without recourse to the bottle. {{right|''A. C. Grant'', Bush-Life in Queensland, I. 30.}}}} '''3.''' In ''U. S. polit. slang'', an opponent of prohibition; one who favors the traffic in liquor.— {{smaller|'''Heavy wet.''' See ''heavy''1.}} '''wet'''1 (wet), ''v. t.''; pret. and pp. ''wetted'' or ''wet'', ppr. ''wetting''.   [< ME. ''weten'', ''wǣten'' (pret. ''wette'', ''watte'', pp. ''wet''), < AS. ''wǣtan'', ''wētan'', ''ge-wētan'' (= Icel. Sw. ''væta'' = Dan. ''væde''), wet, moisten, < ''wǣt'', wet: see ''wet''1, ''a.'']   '''1.''' To make wet; moisten, drench, or soak with water or other fluid; dip or soak in a liquid. {{smaller block|Ne ''wette'' hir fingres in hir sauce depe. {{right|''Chaucer'', Gen. Prol. to C. T., l. 129.}}}} '''2.''' To moisten with drink; hence, figuratively, to inaugurate or celebrate by a drink or a treat of liquor: as, to ''wet'' a new hat. [Slang.] {{smaller block|Down came all the company together, and away! the ale-house was immediately filled with clamour, and scoring one mug to the Marquis of such a place, oil and vinegar to such an Earl, three quarts to my new Lord for ''wetting'' his title. {{right|''Steele'', Spectator, No. 88.}}}} {{smaller block|Then we should have commissions to ''wet''. {{right|''C. Shadwell'', Humours of the Navy, ii. 3.}}}} {{smaller|'''To wet down paper''', in ''printing'', to dip paper in water, or sprinkle it in small portions, which are laid together and left under pressure for a time to allow the moisture to spread equally through the mass. The dampness of the paper fits it for taking the ink readily and evenly in the process of printing, and prevents it from sticking to the type. The finest printing, however, is done with dry paper, and ink of a suitable quality for such use.—'''To wet one’s line.''' See ''line''2.}} {{smaller block|I have not yet ''wetted my line'' since we met together. {{right|''I. Walton'', Complete Angler, p. 84.}}}} {{smaller|'''To wet one’s whistle.''' See ''whistle''.—'''Wetting-out steep.''' Same as ''rot’s steep'' (which see, under ''steep''2).—'''Wetting the block''', among English shoemakers, the act of celebrating by a convivial supper, on the first Monday in March, the cessation of work by candle-light.   ''Halliwell.''}} '''wet2†''', ''v.'' and ''n.''
